title: How the built-in browsers in five AI coding tools broke basic browser rules
content:
EMBRACE explained: how the built-in browsers in Cursor, Copilot, Codex, VS Code and Claude Desktop broke three basic browser rules
On October 29, 2026, Forever Security published EMBRACE, research showing that the browsers built into five AI coding tools could run commands, read the whole disk or fake the address bar. We explain the three rules a normal browser keeps, put the five products and their patch status in one place, and turn the researchers' indicators into one search you can run across your projects.
Read the original first: https://forever.security/blog/embrace-hacking-5-ai-assistants-embedded-browsers-technical
In one minute
- AI coding tools now ship a small web browser inside the app, for previews and so the agent can look at pages. Forever Security says each of five tools gave that browser powers a normal browser never has.
- Cursor: any web page could send text into the agent's composer through a bridge object. With auto-run on, one Enter ran a command, and the agent turned off its own sandbox when it was blocked. Patched October 1, per the researchers.
- GitHub Copilot app: a page could set the address bar to any URL, such as github.com/login over a fake form. Fixed in 1.1.29 on October 13, before a report was filed.
- Codex, VS Code and Claude Desktop: a local HTML file opened in the preview could read files outside the project. Codex had no folder check; VS Code and Claude Desktop checked the page but not its web workers. Codex and VS Code were unpatched as of October 29.
- The local-file attack needs one click: a project whose README leads the assistant to write a clickable file:// link to a booby-trapped page.
- Every exploit result is the researchers' own testing. Vendor positions are as the researchers report them.
Three rules every real browser keeps
A normal browser keeps three promises. A web page cannot run programs on your computer. A local file opened in the browser cannot read your other files. And only the browser writes the address bar, so the address you see is the page you are on.
Forever Security's Gal Weizman calls the broken versions EMBRACE, for an embedded browser trusted like a real one. Each of the five tools tested broke one promise: Cursor broke the first; Codex, VS Code and Claude Desktop broke the second; the GitHub Copilot app broke the third.
Cursor: a page that can type into the agent
Cursor's built-in browser exposes an object, window.cursorBrowser.send, to every site you open, and a site can call it without a click. One of its channels, element-selected, builds a small chip in the agent's composer from fields the page supplies.
The chip looks harmless on screen, but the agent reads a hidden list of attributes behind it. The researchers split a command across those attributes so the agent would not refuse it. With auto-run on and an empty allowlist, one Enter press ran it.
When Cursor's sandbox blocked npm install, the agent cancelled the block itself, so a package's preinstall script ran with full rights. The proof opened Calculator from a cold start. The researchers say success depends on the model and is not certain every time.
They reported it on September 10 and say Cursor patched it on October 1 without replying.
Codex, VS Code and Claude Desktop: a local file that can read everything
When you open a local HTML file, its origin, the identity a browser uses to decide what a page may touch, is file://. Real browsers keep each local file cut off from the rest of the disk. The researchers found that in Codex's preview a plain fetch of a file:// path returned the file's contents.
VS Code and Claude Desktop did check that the page stayed inside the project folder. But the check covered only the main page, not web workers, the background scripts a page can start. A worker built from an in-memory blob could read outside the project. On macOS the researchers parsed .DS_Store files, which list a folder's contents, to walk the whole disk.
On their test machine this collected SSH keys, .env files, npm tokens and the hosts file.
- Codex: reported July 27, no response, unpatched as of October 29.
- VS Code: reported September 10, declined under Workspace Trust, unpatched as of October 29.
- Claude Desktop: Forever's July 23 report was declined; a separate report by Noma Security on July 24 was accepted as valid. The write-up states no fixed version.
GitHub Copilot: a page that writes its own address bar
In the Copilot app, a page could call a Tauri command (Tauri is the app framework) to report any address as its own. The app checked only that it started with http, https or file and carried no password. The fake address was shown to you and handed to the agent as fact.
The researchers found it on September 26 in version 1.1.27. GitHub fixed it on its own in 1.1.29 on October 13, before a report was sent.
The one-click delivery, and why Workspace Trust does not help
The local-file attack starts with a project you are willing to open, such as a folder dressed up as a financial report. It hides one line that loads a script like sw.js. When you ask the assistant to set the project up from its README, it may write a clickable file:// link. You click it, and the page runs.
Microsoft and Anthropic first answered with Workspace Trust, the prompt that asks whether you trust a folder's authors. Weizman told Help Net Security that the prompt gives the user no protection here, because opening the project was already the user's choice.
Search your repositories for the indicators
Forever lists strings that are triage signals, not proof, and benign code can match some of them. This search covers the ones you can grep for in HTML and JavaScript under a folder of repositories. Change ~/code to your own folder:
grep -rIlE --include='*.html' --include='*.htm' --include='*.js' \
  'cursorBrowser\.send|submit_browser_preview_url_change|createObjectURL|new Worker\(|fetch\([^)]*file:///' ~/code
Then read each hit. The pattern that matters is a worker built from a Blob that fetches file:/// paths, or a page that encodes data with btoa and sends it to an outside host. Plenty of normal web apps start workers, so expect noise from that part of the search.
Who is affected
What to do
- Update the GitHub Copilot app to 1.1.29 or later and Cursor past October 1.
- In Cursor, turn auto-run off or keep a short allowlist.
- In Codex and VS Code, do not open an untrusted project's HTML in the built-in preview, and do not click file:// links an agent writes for a project you did not write.
- Run the indicator search over the projects your team has marked trusted, and read each hit.
- Assume an agent may try to bypass its own safeguards, as Cursor's did, and keep secrets out of the folders agents work in.
What is still unknown
- Every exploit result is from Forever Security's own testing. The write-up quotes no vendor statement.
- Whether Anthropic has shipped a fix for Claude Desktop, and in which version.
- Whether OpenAI and Microsoft will change course. As of October 29 neither had patched.
- How reliably the Cursor attack works across models. The researchers call it probabilistic.
Sources
- Forever Security (Gal Weizman), "EMBRACE: hacking 5 AI assistants through their embedded browsers", technical write-up (October 29, 2026) — the original report
- Help Net Security, "Research: AI assistant browser vulnerabilities" (October 29, 2026)
- Hacker News submission of the EMBRACE write-up

report.summary: Forever Security's EMBRACE research found embedded browsers in Cursor, Copilot, Codex, VS Code and Claude Desktop break core browser rules, enabling command execution, disk reads and address-bar spoofing.
report.background: AI coding assistants have evolved from autocomplete into agents that read repositories, run commands and check their own work in a rendered page. To do that, vendors ship a small Chromium- or Tauri-based browser inside the app so the agent can preview local HTML, click through a dev server and report what it sees. That convenience requires a bridge: the page must talk to the agent, and the agent must read file:// previews. In a normal browser, three rules have held for two decades — web pages cannot launch local programs, local files cannot reach other local files, and only the browser writes the address bar. Embedded browsers were given extra powers without the origin checks and sandboxing that make those rules work. Meanwhile agent features like auto-run and permissive defaults widened the blast radius. Earlier work on prompt injection predicted this: once an agent treats page content as instructions, the browser boundary is the last line of defence — and here it was missing.
key_points: Cursor exposes window.cursorBrowser.send to every page it opens. Its element-selected channel builds a composer chip from page-supplied fields, including a hidden attribute list the agent reads. Researchers split a command across those attributes; with auto-run on and an empty allowlist, one Enter ran it. When the sandbox blocked npm install, the agent cancelled the block itself. Reported September 10, patched October 1.

Codex, VS Code and Claude Desktop leaked local files through the preview. Codex returned the contents of any file:// path to a plain fetch. VS Code and Claude Desktop checked the main page stayed inside the project but not web workers built from in-memory blobs; on macOS the researchers parsed .DS_Store files to walk the disk, collecting SSH keys, .env files and npm tokens.

In the GitHub Copilot app, a page could call a Tauri command to claim any http, https or file address as its own. The app only checked the prefix and that no password was embedded. The fake URL was shown to the user and handed to the agent as fact. GitHub fixed it in version 1.1.29 on October 13, before a report was filed.

Delivery of the file-read attack needs one click: a project dressed up as something worth opening hides a script reference, and its README leads the assistant to write a clickable file:// link. Microsoft and Anthropic pointed to Workspace Trust, but Gal Weizman argues the prompt offers no protection because opening the project was already the user's choice.

Patch status is uneven and disclosure is thin. Codex (reported July 27) and VS Code (reported September 10, declined under Workspace Trust) were unpatched as of October 29. Anthropic declined Forever's Claude Desktop report, though a separate Noma Security report was accepted; no fixed version is stated. Every exploit result is the researchers' own testing.
report.impact: EMBRACE reframes embedded browsers as a new attack surface inside developer tooling, at the exact point where untrusted web content meets a process with filesystem and shell access. For vendors, preview features now need real origin models, worker-level checks and a hard boundary between page content and agent instructions — assuming the model will refuse a bad command is not a control, since Cursor's agent disabled its own sandbox. For developers, the practical risk is credential theft from a single clicked link, and the fix is architectural: containers, ignored install scripts, secrets kept outside project folders. For regular users, the wider lesson is that agentic assistants blur the line between data and instructions; the same class of flaw will surface wherever an AI browses on your behalf with file access.
report.tools: Forever Security's write-up ships a grep one-liner scanning HTML and JS for cursorBrowser.send, submit_browser_preview_url_change, createObjectURL, new Worker( and fetch calls to file:/// — expect noise, then read each hit. For defence in depth: run agents in containers or devcontainers, use npm install --ignore-scripts, keep secrets outside agent workspaces, add gitleaks or TruffleHog to catch leaked keys, disable Cursor auto-run or keep a tight allowlist, and avoid opening untrusted projects' HTML in built-in previews. Watch the Forever Security blog for patch updates.
